name: Comfort = Mediocrity
concept: Prospect is comfortable in their current situation, even though it's not where they want to be — the lack of acute pain is preventing them from taking action.
body:
**Comfort = Mediocrity Reframe** — for the prospect who isn't in pain but isn't winning either. The 'just coasting' prospect.

---

"I know that this feels a little uncomfortable, but this is the way it's got to be.

Comfort is the breeding ground for mediocrity.

So you can either stay in that breeding ground for another 12, 18 months — or we can start to make the moves so we can start to become the person we wanna be in order to get the results.

It's up to you. At the end of the day, it's your choice.

So — what do YOU need to get the outcomes that you want for you, your business, and your family?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Late call. Use when the prospect lacks urgency because their current state isn't catastrophic — they're comfortable enough that change feels harder than staying.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "I'm doing okay, I just want to do better."
- "It's not urgent, I'm not desperate."
- "I'm comfortable enough — I just want to grow."
- Prospect treating the call as exploratory rather than action-oriented.

**The mechanism:** Reframes comfort itself as the enemy. Most prospects think 'comfortable' is good. This analogy makes comfort sound like a slow death — 'breeding ground for mediocrity' is a phrase they'll remember for weeks. The closing question pivots into self-determination (their family, their choice), not your pitch.

name: The Right Teacher
concept: Prospect believes they don't need help / can do it on their own / has tried similar things before and concluded it just doesn't work for them.
body:
**The Right Teacher** — for early-call prospects who say "I think I'll just give this a try on my own" or who've tried similar solutions and given up.

---

"Yeah, that makes sense. Now — would you say that you've tried things in the past, and, you know, you've given it a red-hot crack? Yes? Do you feel like you gave it a good crack? Yes?

Okay, cool. So if you've tried everything in the past, and you did it the right way, and it just didn't work out — then maybe there's something going on, like me. I'm dyslexic, right?

And so I was in all the lowest classes when I was a kid. Until a teacher came around that knew how to teach me. And then I went to upper class, and I ended up graduating salutatorian — all that kind of good stuff.

And so it wasn't that I was dumb. It's just that I hadn't been taught the way that I needed to be taught. And it wasn't even that the teaching style was wrong, because it was right for almost everybody — just not me.

Would you be open to maybe considering that it's not that there's anything wrong with those approaches you tried before — but maybe that you're just one of those, say, two or three percent of people that react differently to things, or need some tinkering, and you just haven't found the right teacher yet to come in and teach you the right way?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Early-call. Discovery / engagement phase. Used when prospects say things like "I think I'll just try this on my own" or "I've tried things like this before and they didn't work."

**Trigger situations this handles:**
- "I'll just give this a try on my own."
- "I've tried programs / coaches / courses like this before — didn't work."
- Upselling buyer leads from low-ticket into high-ticket.
- Prospects who are skeptical because of past failed attempts.

**The mechanism:** It turns past failure into evidence of needing the right teacher (you), not evidence that the prospect is broken. Makes them a "special little snowflake" — their failure isn't lack of effort, it's lack of fit.

**Sits in the same toolbox as:**
- 🏝️ Desert Island Syndrome → handles "this is a stretch."
- 🏢 Penthouse / Ground Floor → handles "let me think about it."
- 🏃 Usain Bolt → sets up vision + consequence questions.
- 📚 The Right Teacher → handles "I've tried this before / I'll do it on my own."
- 🕳️ Cave Vision → handles "I already know what to do."

**Don't use this if** the prospect has zero past experience with the problem — there's nothing to reframe.

name: The Orchestra vs. The Mosh Pit
concept: Why synchronized channels beat more channels
body:
One-line: More channels without sync isn't a symphony — it's a mosh pit with instruments.

Extended: Picture two rooms. Room A: 40 world-class musicians, no conductor, everyone playing their own song. Room B: 4 musicians, one sheet of music, one conductor. Which one do you want to listen to? That's your pipeline on duct tape vs. your pipeline on a Lead State.
useWhen: Everyone intuitively knows a 40-piece orchestra with no conductor sounds worse than a 4-piece band in sync. Makes the abstract idea of 'synchronization' physically obvious. Use when teaching the Synchronized Journey Framework or explaining why more channels without coordination underperforms.

name: The Bitcoin Time Machine
concept: Prospect intellectually sees the opportunity but isn't feeling the urgency — they're treating a window-of-opportunity decision like a routine one.
body:
**The Bitcoin Time Machine** — for the prospect who can SEE the opportunity but won't ACT on it. Used to create future-regret without sounding pushy.

---

"Let me ask you something. If I gave you a time machine right now — just for ten minutes — and I sent you back to 2010, where you could find your past self… what would you tell them?

Because Bitcoin in 2010 was about eight cents. Eight cents. Today it's worth tens of thousands of dollars per coin. So if you could go back, sit your past self down, and say 'mate, take everything you've got. Every dollar. Every bit of savings. Put it into this weird internet money called Bitcoin. Don't ask why. Just do it.'

What do you reckon your past self would say?

They'd probably go 'nah, that sounds risky. I don't really get it. I'll think about it. Maybe next year when I've got a bit more.'

And you'd want to shake them, right? Because YOU can see what they can't. You can see what was on the other side of that decision. You can see the house they could've bought. The freedom they could've had. The life they could've built. And from where you're standing now, it's so obvious.

But here's the thing — the past version of you wasn't being stupid. They were just making the decision with the information they had. They couldn't see what you can see now. That's the only difference.

So — if a future version of you, ten years from now, could come back to this conversation right now… what do you reckon they'd be telling you to do?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Solution awareness phase / pre-pitch / setting up the close. Mid-call. Used BEFORE the price reveal or BEFORE the close, to install future regret as a decision-making lens.

**Trigger situations this handles:**
- Prospect can articulate the opportunity but isn't urgent.
- Prospect treats a window-of-opportunity decision like a routine one.
- Prospect says "I want to think about it" on something time-sensitive.
- Prospect understands the offer logically but isn't feeling it.
- Setting up a consequence question without making it feel heavy.

**The mechanism:** It uses HINDSIGHT BIAS in reverse. The prospect already knows that past-them would've made the wrong call on Bitcoin. So when you ask "what would future-you tell present-you to do?" — they answer it themselves, in their own voice, and that answer becomes their commitment.

**Sits in the same toolbox as:**
- 🏃 Usain Bolt at the YMCA → sets up vision + consequence questions.
- ⏳ Bitcoin Time Machine → installs future-regret / hindsight as the decision lens.
- 🏝️ Desert Island Syndrome → closes when objection is financial.

**Don't use this if:**
- The prospect has actual reason to wait (legitimate timing constraints).
- The opportunity isn't actually time-sensitive (this analogy IMPLIES urgency — don't fake it).
- The prospect didn't live through Bitcoin's rise (substitute a different asset — see variations).

name: The Plane Ticket
concept: Prospect can't see themselves on the other side of the destination — they're trying to figure out HOW the program works before they commit to whether they're getting on the plane.
body:
**Plane Ticket Reframe** — for the prospect who's stuck on "how is this going to work?" / "I can't see how I get from here to there" / "I'd like to do it myself."

---

"It's completely normal that the other side doesn't make sense. It is completely normal that you're having a disconnect seeing yourself at that destination. It's not your job to know exactly how you're gonna get there.

When you buy a plane ticket, you don't go to the pilot and say, 'Hey pilot, let me take a look around your cockpit because I want to make sure that you know how to get me from London to New York.'

That's not your responsibility. It's the pilot's responsibility to get you from London to New York. Your only responsibility is to show up on your flight.

Show up on your flight, strap on your seat belt, and let's go for this ride. And as long as you can do that — as long as you can buy your ticket and show up — we'll do the rest. We'll bring you to your destination.

But you gotta show up. You gotta buy the ticket. You gotta hop on the flight, and you have to come along for the ride.

Are you willing to do that?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Late objection handling. Used when prospect understands the offer logically but can't see themselves on the other side, or when they want to micromanage HOW the result happens before committing.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "I can't see how this will work for me."
- "How exactly does this work? Walk me through every step."
- "I'm a do-it-myself kind of person."
- "I need to understand the whole roadmap before I commit."
- Fear of the Unknown.

**The mechanism:** Re-allocates responsibility. Right now they're trying to do BOTH the buyer's job (decide to go) AND the pilot's job (figure out the route). The analogy puts those back in the right hands. They only have to do their part.

name: Usain Bolt at the YMCA
concept: Prospect won't articulate what's at stake or what they're chasing — making it impossible to ask sharp consequence or vision questions.
body:
**Usain Bolt at the YMCA** — a setup analogy that makes prospects WANT to tell you what they're chasing and what's on the line. Used in the solution-awareness phase.

---

"Let's just say we put Usain Bolt on the 100-metre line, and he's at the local YMCA. He's gonna run pretty quick. He's a fast runner. But let's just say I put him on the 100-metre line and it's the gold medal on the line. It's the Olympics. There's millions and millions of people watching. And you hit that gun, and he goes — he's gonna run faster.

Because he knows exactly what he's running for, right? He can taste it. He can feel it. It's led up to this point. All those people are watching. It's a huge moment. So he's gonna run even faster now.

And you know what — if I released a lion behind him? He'd probably run even faster again, right?

So — what is that gold medal for you? What are you actually chasing?

[After they answer]

Okay. And what's the lion? What happens if you don't figure this out, you don't do anything about this, you never even get to be in the gold medal race?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Solution awareness phase. Mid-call. Used to set up vision questions AND consequence questions (the lion is the consequence question).

**Trigger situations this handles:**
- Prospect is being vague about their goals.
- Prospect won't articulate the cost of inaction.
- You as the rep find consequence questions awkward to ask cold.
- You need them to verbalise the stakes so they buy in to their own outcome.

**The structural genius:** This analogy gives you PERMISSION to ask both vision (gold medal) and consequence (lion) questions in the same beat — which is normally a high-friction sequence. The analogy makes it natural.

**Don't use this if** they've already articulated stakes clearly. It'd be redundant and feel like you're not listening.

name: Penthouse / Ground Floor
concept: Prospect wants to 'go away and think about it' — they're trying to make a decision from their current vantage point, which is too low to see the full picture.
body:
**Penthouse / Ground Floor Reframe** — for the prospect who says "I just need to think about it" / "let me sleep on it" / "I want to mull it over."

---

"Okay, well that makes sense kind of based off where you're at, right?

But the only problem is — if you're always making decisions based off where you are, then where you are is the only place you can ever be. Does that make sense?

Let's just say you're at the penthouse. You're really high. You can see a lot. You can intake a lot of information. But if you're at the ground floor, you can't see anywhere near as far. So the amount of information you can intake is much less.

So if I had to get from one place to another, I'm in a much better position if I have a higher perspective — because I can intake more information.

But to get that perspective, you have to make the decisions of the person that got to the penthouse.

So — what are the things that you feel like you need to do to put yourself in the right position to where you can kind of make that shift?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Objection handling, specifically post-logistics, when shifting from logistical objections (money/time) into fear-based objections.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "I need to think about it."
- "Let me sleep on it."
- "I want to mull it over."
- "I'll get back to you."

**Sits in the same toolbox as:**
- 🏝️ Desert Island Syndrome → handles "this is a stretch."
- 🏢 Penthouse / Ground Floor → handles "let me think about it."
- 🕳️ Cave Vision → handles "I already know what to do."

**Why this works:** It opens the first little door. Matt's framework: feel → think → do. You can't make them buy on a 'think about it' — you first have to shift them from "I need to think about it" to "I need to think about it differently." That's the entire job of this analogy.

**Don't use this if** they have a real, specific reason to delay (need to talk to spouse, board approval, etc.) — use Third Party Reframe instead.

name: Perfect Strategy for Where You Are
concept: Prospect can't see beyond their current situation and is unconsciously running patterns that keep them stuck. They believe their current state is just 'how things are' rather than the result of specific decisions.
body:
**Perfect Strategy Reframe** — for the prospect who unconsciously thinks their current results are just life, not the predictable output of their patterns.

---

"Right now, you've got the perfect strategy to be exactly where you're meant to be.

Whatever you're doing — it's perfectly fine, based on your decisions, thoughts, feelings, actions, and the meaning you've attached to everything in your life.

We, as humans, are perfectly designed to be where we are meant to be. You've been running an unconscious strategy and unconscious patterns of thinking that have led you up to this point.

If you would like to change that pattern — it's going to require a new YOU. A new way of thinking, new actions, new skills, new capabilities. Otherwise, you will never be able to change.

Right?

So if you continue to make decisions based on who you are right now, you'll never change — and you'll always have what you have.

But if you do, that's totally fine by me. I just don't think that's what's best for you.

Do you?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Mid-to-late call. Mindset reframe. Use when prospect is fatalistic about their current results — 'this is just how it is for me.'

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "I've always been this way."
- "This is just how it is in my industry / situation."
- "I don't think I can change."
- Prospect describes their current state as fixed rather than chosen.

**The mechanism:** Reframes 'where you are' from VICTIM to ARCHITECT. The prospect's current life is the OUTPUT of a perfect strategy — perfect for getting them exactly where they currently are. To get somewhere else, you need a different perfect strategy. This puts agency back in their hands.

name: Desert Island Syndrome
concept: Prospect feels the offer is a stretch — financial, time, or commitment-wise — and is about to back out because of the discomfort of the push.
body:
**Desert Island Syndrome Reframe** — for the prospect who says "this is a stretch" / "this is a lot" / "I'd have to really push to make this work."

---

"Okay, I hear you and I appreciate that things may be a stretch for you, and we have had many people in the same circumstances as you. In fact it's that common that we call it the 'Desert Island Syndrome.' Can I explain why?

Imagine you were trapped on a desert island and you had made a raft in order to break free and escape into the open ocean. What part of the process of getting free would be the most challenging?

It's breaking past the surf, right?

And that's where you are now — your current circumstances are like the waves pushing you back, stopping you. But the truth is, you are so close to success and one solid push and you are away. Free.

It means packing everything you have on the raft, putting your head down, and just going for it and throwing everything at the surf. Because if you don't, the surf's just gonna keep on pushing you back to the island forever, and it's okay for now — but your resources and your desire are just gonna dwindle. Does that kinda make sense?

Look, I can help you make this stretch so you can break free. Are you in?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Objection handling — specifically the "this is a stretch" / financial commitment objection.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "This is a real stretch for me right now."
- "I'd have to really push to make this work."
- "I don't know if I can swing it."
- "This is more than I was expecting / planning to spend."

**Sits in the same toolbox as:**
- 🏝️ Desert Island Syndrome → handles "this is a stretch."
- 🏢 Penthouse / Ground Floor → handles "let me think about it."
- 🕳️ Cave Vision → handles "I already know what to do."

**Don't use this if** the prospect is already excited and pushing forward — the analogy implies hardship and can deflate momentum.

name: The Leaky Bucket of Leads
concept: Why fixing friction beats buying more traffic
body:
One-line: Buying more traffic with a leaky pipeline is pouring faster water into a bucket with six holes.

Extended: Every dollar of ad spend is a pour. Every unreminded lead, generic follow-up, and broken transition is a hole. You don't need a bigger hose, you need to patch the holes first — then the same pour fills the bucket.
useWhen: Anchors the Friction Leak Map visually. Nobody argues with 'pour less water into a leaky bucket.' Use during the Problem Frame section when walking through friction leaks.

name: Cave Vision
concept: Prospect believes they already know what they need to do — they've pattern-matched their problem to a familiar solution and don't think they need a new perspective.
body:
**Cave Vision Reframe** — for the prospect who says "I already know what I need to do" / "I've figured it out" / "I just need to execute on my plan."

---

"Okay, I hear you, and I appreciate you've thought about this and you reckon you've got a handle on what you need to do. We get this one a lot — common enough that we've actually got a name for it. We call it 'Cave Vision.' Can I explain why?

Imagine for a sec — you've spent your whole life sitting in a cave. Facing a wall. And on that wall, you can see shadows moving around, and you've got really, really good at reading those shadows. You know which shadow means food, which one means danger, which one means rain's coming. You've basically mastered the wall. Make sense?

Now — what you don't know is that behind you, there's a fire. And behind the fire, there's a whole world. Sun. Trees. Other people. Real things casting those shadows. You've never seen any of it. All you've ever known is the wall.

So when someone walks in and goes 'mate, you've got to come outside, there's a whole world out here' — what do you reckon happens? You fight 'em. Right? Because in your world, the wall is everything. The shadows are real. And anyone telling you different is either crazy or trying to trick you.

Here's the thing though — it's not that you're wrong about the shadows. You've read those shadows better than anyone. The problem is just that the shadows are a really small slice of what's actually going on. And until someone walks you out, you don't even know what you don't know. Does that kinda make sense?

So when you say 'I've thought about this and I know what I need to do' — I believe you. You've been reading your own wall for a long time. But part of what we'd actually be doing together is just walking you out of the cave for a sec. Not telling you the wall doesn't matter — just showing you what's casting the shadows. And once you see it, you can't unsee it, and then your decisions get a lot easier.

Would you be open to at least having a look at what's outside before you decide?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Objection handling, post-logistics, when shifting into fear/identity.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "I already know what I need to do."
- "I've figured it out — I just need to execute."
- "I've thought about this a lot already."
- "I've tried this kind of thing before / I know what works for me."

**Sits in the same toolbox as:**
- 🏝️ Desert Island Syndrome → handles "this is a stretch."
- 🏢 Penthouse / Ground Floor → handles "let me think about it."
- 🕳️ Cave Vision → handles "I already know what to do."

Three reframes, three different objections, no overlap.

**Don't use this if** the prospect is genuinely informed and has done the work — they'll feel patronised. Best on prospects who are confidently wrong, not confidently right.

name: Fork in the Road
concept: Prospect can't see beyond their current situation — they keep recreating the same reality but want different results.
body:
**Fork in the Road Reframe** — for the prospect whose current decision-making process got them where they are, but they want to be somewhere else.

---

"Okay, so I can understand that this is a big move for you and that you might need to think about it or take some time. May I ask you a question?

Do you feel your mindset and decision-making process have got you to where you are today?

[Yes]

Okay. And are you 100% happy with where you are at with [XYZ] right now?

[Well, no]

Okay. And do you want that decision-making process to dictate your results moving forward into the future?

[No, I don't]

Why not?

[They explain]

So — I guess this is a fork in the road, buddy. Stay where you are, keep recreating the same reality. Or get the new skills and knowledge and get where you want to go.

Which is it going to be?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Late objection handling. Use when prospect says "I need to think about it" but you've already used Penthouse OR when their hesitation is mindset-based, not money-based.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "I need to think about it" (after Penthouse already deployed).
- Prospect describes wanting different results but defending their current process.
- "I'm just not sure if this is right for me."

**The mechanism:** Self-incrimination via Socratic questioning. By the time they answer the third question, they've ALREADY conceded that their current decision-making process isn't getting them what they want — in their own voice. The fork question is just naming what's already on the table.

name: The Finish Line
concept: Prospect is wobbling at the very end of the call — they've agreed to everything logically but are about to bail right before the close.
body:
**Finish Line Reframe** — for the prospect who's about to bail at the eleventh hour. Last-resort close.

---

"That's okay if you want to think about it. But I don't think that's what's best for you given the information you told me a moment ago.

We're right at the finish line — and this is where so many people stop and bail.

But here's the thing: you're going to have to eventually do it. Whether it's now, tomorrow, one year, or ten years. And each time you delay, the problem is just gonna get worse.

Committing is the hardest thing about this. After this point, all you need to do is follow our lead, take each day as it comes, and get the results that you have been searching for.

Are you in?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** End-of-call. Last-minute wobble. ONLY use when you've already deployed 1–2 other reframes and they're still hesitating right at the close.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "Let me think about it" (after Penthouse + Fork in the Road have failed).
- Vague last-minute hesitation.
- Prospect agrees logically but emotionally pulling back.

**The mechanism:** Acknowledges this is the hard part (validation), reframes delay as compounding cost (consequence), then makes commitment seem like the SMALL part vs. all the work after (re-anchors effort).

**Don't use this if:**
- It's early-call (premature, looks pushy).
- Prospect has a specific concrete reason to delay (use Third Party or Real Reason reframes).
- You haven't earned the right — you need 30+ minutes of rapport before "that's not what's best for you" lands.

name: Bad First Boyfriend
concept: Prospect has been burned before by a similar program / coach / investment and is letting one bad past experience block a different future opportunity.
body:
**Bad First Boyfriend Reframe** — for the prospect who's been burned before and is using past trauma as the reason to stay still.

---

"I sense that you may have had some bad experiences in the past relating to [X]. May I ask you a question?

When you were 15 — or that sort of age — did you have a real crappy boyfriend or girlfriend? One who hurt you, dumped you, cheated on you, or in some other way?

[Yes]

And has that stopped you from going out and finding a decent person and enjoying connection and partnership with someone since?

Or did you stay single?

[No, of course not / I moved on]

Right. So — are you going to let the memory of one bad experience stop you from experiencing the benefits of [the program] that will allow you to achieve [XYZ]?"
useWhen:
**Phase:** Objection handling. Use when prospect references a past failed coaching / program / investment as the reason they're hesitating.

**Trigger objections this handles:**
- "I bought a course like this once and it didn't work."
- "I've worked with a coach before and got burned."
- "I've tried programs like this before — they're all the same."
- "I'm gun-shy after my last experience."

**The mechanism:** Universalises their fear (everyone had a bad first relationship), shows them they ALREADY know how to recover from it (they didn't stay single), then transposes that recovery onto the buying decision. Self-evident logic, no convincing required.

concept: Prospect believes they already know what they need to do — they've pattern-matched their problem to a familiar solution and don't think they need a new perspective.
